design: The authors collected message data (text, images, video, audio, URLs) from 227 public WhatsApp groups in Pakistan between January 10 and mid-April 2020 using Selenium automation and a rooted Android device to decrypt the local SQLite database, alongside 800,000 COVID-19-related tweets from Twitter collected from January 10 to April 9, 2020.
integrity_note: The venue (IEEE ASONAM 2020), author affiliations, detailed methodology (Selenium, rooted Android, SQLite decryption), ethics note, and real references all indicate a genuine study. However, multiple numerical inconsistencies require human verification: Table I percentages for URLs (2.5% vs actual 5.3%) and Others (5.4% vs actual 11.2%) do not match their counts, and the 'Others' row appears to be excluded from the 60,202 total despite being listed; Table IV sums to 620 images but the text claims 541 COVID-related images were found; Table III sums to 645 misinformation texts but Table II reports only 596; and the claimed 14% misinformation rate (abstract/Figure 3) conflicts with the 11.3% calculable from Table II. These are likely reporting errors rather than fabrication, but they prevent the tables from being reconciled with the text.

design: The study collected approximately 53 million Twitter tweets and retweets in six languages (English, Japanese, Spanish, French, German, Korean) containing 16 keywords and their translations via the Twitter REST API v1.1 from February 24 to March 12, 2022, then used network analysis to tag pro-Russian users and text embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, UMAP, k-means) to cluster highly retweeted tweets and identify misinformation topics.
integrity_note: Venue is Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio, DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-60653-y), a legitimate indexed journal with a standard editorial timeline (received 14 Dec 2023, accepted 25 Apr 2024). All quantitative claims reconcile: the six language volumes (30.5M+11.8M+7.5M+1.7M+0.571M+0.690M=52.761M) sum to the stated ~53 million total; the pro-Russian user counts (220K+40K+177K+26K+7K+120=470,120) sum to the stated ~470K and represent 62% of the 9.2M total population, consistent with the claimed 60-70% tagging rate; and every percentage in Table 3 (43%, 35%, 35%, 35%, 21%, 33%) matches its count and base within rounding (e.g., 708,783/1,645,338=43.1%, 344/1,055=32.6%≈33%). Methods are described with sufficient specificity (API version, date range, keyword list, network tagging procedure, embedding model, clustering) to have been executed as reported, and the prose is technical and specific rather than generic.

design: The study collected public social media messages about health topics (vaccines, nutrition, Ebola) from Twitter, Facebook, and Reddit (last ten days of extraction for Twitter; last 100 posts for Facebook; specific Reddit conversations), selecting the top 100 tweets per hashtag, top 20 posts and 20 comments per Facebook page, and selected Reddit comments for a final coded sample of 450 messages.
integrity_note: Venue is the legitimate, indexed MDPI journal IJERPH (Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health). Table 4 percentages sum to 100–101% (within rounding error). SICOR values in Table 5 reconcile with the reported counts (e.g., Twitter ESISM 39+18+4=61 of 300 = 20.3% → 20%; Facebook 6 of 80 = 7.5% → 8%). The stated N=453/450 is consistent with the SICOR denominators despite ambiguous wording in Table 2's Reddit row (likely an extraction artefact). Specific verbatim quotes from social media and detailed ethical/methodological descriptions indicate genuine data collection; no signs of fabrication, predatory venue, or impossible numbers.

design: A registered-report online survey of 1,010 U.S. adults who use social media at least weekly, fielded July–August 2024 via Cloud Research/Mechanical Turk, measuring self-reported effort levels when responding to misinformation posted by close, somewhat close, and not-close contacts and by oneself.
integrity_note: Venue is legitimate (Scientific Reports, Nature Portfolio, indexed in DOAJ and Core). The study is a registered report with a verifiable Stage 1 protocol (accepted March 13, 2024), IRB approval (STUDY2022_00000143), and a specific data-collection window (July–August 2024). All percentages in Table 4 reconcile exactly with their counts and base of 1,010 (942/1010=93.3%, 68/1010=6.7%, 260/1010=25.7%, 750/1010=74.3%). Sample sizes in Table 5 are internally consistent as overlapping subsets of the 1,010 participants (e.g., 148+370+880=1,398 closeness-level observations from 942 participants who saw misinformation; H2.1 n=256 is consistent with the 260 who admitted posting). The only anomaly is the 'Received: 15 February 2023' date, which conflicts with the 2024 data collection but is almost certainly a typo for 2025 and does not indicate fabricated data.

design: The study collected Arabic-language tweets geolocated in Saudi Arabia (13 June–12 July 2020) via the Twitter standard search API, Google Trends search-volume time series for Saudi provinces (February–July 2020), Google Community Mobility Reports (16 February–25 June 2020), and official daily COVID-19 case counts from the Saudi Ministry of Health, then analyzed correlations and ran multiple regression models predicting new cases.
integrity_note: All quantitative results are internally consistent: the four Twitter term counts (3807, 1694, 1021, 19) sum exactly to the reported total of 6541 tweets, and their percentages (58.2%, 26%, 15.6%, 0.3%) match the counts. The regression variance components sum correctly to the reported R² values (88.31% and 89.16%). Methods specify concrete tools (Python 3.7.0, Tweepy, Farasa, Tashaphyne), dates (13 June–12 July 2020 for Twitter; Feb–July 2020 for Trends; 16 Feb–25 June 2020 for mobility), and data sources (Saudi Ministry of Health dashboard). The venue is a legitimate indexed MDPI journal with matching author affiliations. Minor factual slips (the 275,000-case date and the residential-mobility direction) appear to be typos in the narrative, not signs that the underlying data were fabricated.

design: The study collected approximately 7.2 million COVID-19 vaccine-related tweets and associated user metadata from Twitter between November 2020 and May 2021 using a scraper and the Twitter API, then applied a semi-supervised LinearSVC model with active learning to classify misinformation and used the M3-inference model and Botometer API to profile account demographics and bot-like activity.
integrity_note: The paper contains irreconcilable internal contradictions: Methods report 7,235,159 tweets from 2,223,969 users while Results report 7,235,182 tweets from 2,223,182 users; the Abstract claims misinformation spreaders had '15% more astroturf bot activity' but the Results state the astroturf score was 'twice' that of fact-spreaders (0.25 vs 0.12, a ~100% difference, not 15%); and the Discussion cites a misinformation low in 'February and March, 2020,' which predates the stated November 2020–May 2021 study window. These discrepancies—especially the changing sample sizes and the misreported headline percentage—indicate the data are not reported consistently and may not be trustworthy as presented.

design: The study collected 259,176 original Brazilian Portuguese tweets containing COVID-19 hashtags (#coronavirus OR #covid OR #covid19) between April and June 2020 via the Twitter API, classified them for fake-news content using a deep-learning model (92% accuracy) trained on a web-scraped repository of 12,200 fact-checked news items (3,100 fake, 9,100 non-fake), and analyzed sharing (retweet counts) and adoption (like counts) across verified and unverified accounts using chi-square tests of independence.
integrity_note: Venue is legitimate: SN Computer Science is a Springer Nature journal indexed in Scopus/Web of Science (is_core: True), with a valid DOI and appropriate scope for a computational social-science study. All quantitative claims reconcile: 337,403 retrieved minus exclusions yields 259,176 analyzed; the news repository sums correctly (3,100 + 9,100 = 12,200); every row in Tables 2 and 3 sums exactly to its stated total (e.g., 255,526 + 2,988 + 662 = 259,176; 191,490 + 12,257 + 51,779 = 255,526), and all percentages match their counts within standard rounding. The methodology (Twitter API key, specific hashtags, date range April–June 2020, Brazilian Portuguese filter, exclusion of retweets/duplicates/bots, 70/30 train-test split, ANN architecture, chi-square df values) is described with sufficient operational detail to have been executed as reported. No signals of fabricated data, impossible splits, AI-filler prose, or venue/topic mismatch were detected.

design: Qualitative content analysis of 1,963 systematically sampled social media contributions (plus 300 most-viral posts) from Twitter, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook and blogs, collected via Ubermetrics during July–December 2021 in Switzerland and manually coded using Mayring's method.
integrity_note: Venue is legitimate (European Journal of Health Communication, University of Zurich; indexed in DOAJ and CORE). All reported percentages reconcile with their bases: the three statement categories sum to 100% (52+32+16); Figure 2 bars sum to 99.9% (rounding); Tables 1–5 sub-items sum to their category totals within 0.1% rounding; the margin-of-error calculation in note 16 is arithmetically correct (1.96×√(0.443×0.557/688)=0.037). Figure 4 percentages exceed 100% only because multiple issues per statement are permitted (consistent with Tables 1–5 collectively summing to >100%). Methods are transparent (reliability scores, data availability, funding, ethics statement). Minor typo in methods ('August to December' vs July data reported in Figure 3) is a wording slip, not evidence of fabrication.

design: An online quantitative survey distributed via Google Forms (active for 12 days) collected data from 163 respondents (162 analyzed after excluding one) on demographics, social media habits, news consumption, and exposure to 20 fake news items.
integrity_note: The data are likely not real as reported: both age groups report an identical mean fake news exposure of 8.1 (implausible for n=35 vs n=120 and suggesting copied statistics); age group definitions contradict each other (18–35 vs 18–34 vs 35+); multiple categorical counts fail to sum to group totals (e.g., urban/rural 24+10=34≠35; time-spent 7+4+4+5=20≠35, leaving 15 unaccounted); and venue metadata is inconsistent (publisher listed as SAGE but DOI prefix 10.15655 is not SAGE's, and the journal is not in DOAJ despite claiming core status).

design: The study collected quantitative and qualitative data from 50 YouTube videos (selected from 120 identified via 12 search terms on November 3, 2021) assessing video source, engagement metrics (views, likes, dislikes, comments), length, upload date, and quality using a modified DISCERN score and global quality score, with the 10 most-viewed videos further analyzed for messaging and format.
integrity_note: Published in a legitimate core journal (Journal of Endodontics, Elsevier) with a valid DOI, real institutional affiliations, ethics approval, a specific data-collection date, and internally consistent counts (12 search terms × 10 = 120 identified; 50 analyzed; Table 2 source counts sum to 50; Table 3 row counts sum to overall totals). Two minor percentage mismatches in Table 3 (16/50 reported as 30.0% instead of 32.0%; 2/31 reported as 6.2% instead of 6.5%) appear to be typographical errors rather than fabrication. No signals of predatory venue, AI-generated filler, topic mismatch, or impossible data.

design: The authors downloaded all posts from the Usenet newsgroup sci.med.pharmacy dated April 29 to May 19, 1995 (downloaded on May 19, 1995), extracted 310 nonsubjective drug information statements, and had two University of New Mexico pharmacy students independently classify each statement for accuracy (correct/incorrect/could not verify) and potential harm (no/minor/moderate/severe) using standard references (AHFS, USP DI, Goodman & Gilman), with disagreements resolved by a faculty member.
integrity_note: All counts and percentages reconcile across Tables 2-4 and the text: 160+111+39=310 (Table 2); 211+23+29+8+39=310 (Table 3); Table 4 columns sum to 160 correct, 111 incorrect, 39 not verified; 51.6%+35.8%+12.6%=100%; harmful categories 7.4%+9.4%+2.6%=19.4%; disagreement 65/310=21.0%. The venue is a legitimate core pharmacy journal (J Am Pharm Assoc, Elsevier, ISSN 1086-5802), the methods describe a specific 20-day download of a real newsgroup with named reference standards and reviewer adjudication, and the quoted newsgroup statements in Table 1 are specific and contextually authentic. The abstract phrase 'one-fifth of the incorrect recommendations' appears to be a wording imprecision for the 19.4% harmful rate of total statements (Results section), not a data fabrication.

design: Social media metrics (likes, members, followers, views, comments, duration) for hyperacusis-related content on Facebook pages/groups, Twitter accounts, and YouTube videos were manually scraped by two independent reviewers using the keyword 'hyperacusis' between 16 July 2017 and 9 August 2017.
integrity_note: The paper is published in a legitimate Taylor & Francis journal (Hearing, Balance and Communication, CORE-indexed) with a valid DOI and real institutional affiliations (Hofstra University, St. John's University). The study describes a specific, reproducible data collection protocol (keyword 'hyperacusis', dates 16 July–9 August 2017, defined inclusion thresholds, two independent reviewers, private browsing mode). All sample sizes, totals, and percentages reconcile correctly (e.g., 84+59+7+5=155; 84/155=54.19%; 48,015/59=814; 4252/7=607.42). Two descriptive statistics contain calculation errors (mean comments reported as 5 instead of 66.15; mean dislikes for information sharing reported as 3.73 instead of 2.73), but these appear to be isolated typos in derived statistics rather than evidence of fabricated data, as the underlying totals and counts are internally consistent and match the text.

design: The study collected 809,072 tweets containing 'ibuprofen'/'ibuprofeno'/'ibuprofene' from March 11–28, 2020 via the Twitter API, filtered these to 213,567 tweets across five European countries plus Catalonia, manually coded the top 25 tweets per language (152 total) for misinformation and author type, and separately analyzed 1,401 Catalan users' following of official accounts versus their sharing of misinformation.
integrity_note: The venue is legitimate (Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review, DOAJ/CORE indexed, CC BY 4.0) and the study design is plausible, but the results contain internal numerical inconsistencies: Table 1 and Table 2 disagree on the distribution of Fake credible vs. Generic tweets (17/38 vs. 15/40), Table 1 percentages do not match its own counts (41/101=40.6% not 39.6%), and the text's claim of a 70% baseline probability and 60% reduction in Finding 4 contradicts Table 3/Table 5 (actual: 94% baseline, 61% when following, a 33-point drop). These suggest reporting errors rather than fabrication, but the data as reported cannot be fully reconciled.

design: The study collected 1.59 million Italian-language Facebook posts containing COVID-19 keywords shared by 87,426 public pages/groups between January 1 and May 12, 2020, using CrowdTangle's historical data interface, along with engagement metrics and URLs.
integrity_note: Table 1 contains two percentage mismatches beyond rounding: the intersection posts count (39) is listed as 0.024% but calculates to 0.0025%, and the union accounts count (15,865) is listed as 28.8% but calculates to 28.1%. The abstract also states 'nearly 80k' accounts while the methods report 87,426. These inconsistencies suggest calculation or reporting errors warranting human review, though the detailed methodology, specific network metrics (e.g., 983,582 vertices), and legitimate venue (Elsevier's Online Social Networks and Media) indicate genuine data collection.

design: Infodemiology content analysis of 500 English and 500 Brazilian Portuguese Facebook posts about dental caries, collected via CrowdTangle on August 26, 2021 (covering August 2016–August 2021), and manually characterized by two independent investigators for author profile, sentiment, motivation, aim, and facticity.
integrity_note: Legitimate USP dissertation with detailed, plausible methods and claimed open data, but multiple table inconsistencies (wrong percentage in Table 3 Article 1; identical rows in Table 2 Article 1; identical statistics for different categories in Table 1 Article 1) indicate possible copy-paste errors in reporting that require human verification of the underlying dataset.

design: The study collected self-report survey data from 2,506 U.S. Twitter users (recruited via CloudResearch between August 2022 and February 2023) and 7,713,506 of their historical Twitter engagements from December 2019 to December 2021 (retrieved via the academic API between January and March 2023), which were classified using machine learning for support of six COVID-19 conspiracy theories.
integrity_note: Published in Nature Communications (legitimate CORE journal, DOAJ-indexed, Nature Portfolio). All reported counts reconcile with their percentages (e.g., 20,705/7,713,506 = 0.268% ≈ 0.27%; 153/7,713,506 = 0.002% ≈ 0.00%; engagement breakdown 3,607,354 + 1,012,565 + 1,084,863 + 2,008,724 = 7,713,506). Odds ratios in the text match the tables exactly (e.g., Table 1 Age OR=1.86 reported as '86% more likely'; Table 4 Age OR=2.36 reported as '136% more likely'). Ethics approval number, informed consent, and precise data collection windows (survey Aug 2022–Feb 2023; Twitter data Dec 2019–Dec 2021, extracted Jan–Mar 2023) are explicitly documented. Machine learning classification is validated against human raters (n=1,019 for similarity model, n=1,136 for support model) with reported PABAK, precision, recall, and F1 metrics. Data and code are deposited on OSF with a detailed restricted-access protocol for raw Twitter data. No evidence of fabricated data, impossible splits, or venue mismatch.

design: Analysis of 52 YouTube videos in Portuguese containing vaccine misinformation/disinformation, collected via YouTube Data Tools on February 10, 2020 (triplicate extraction yielding 1,714, 2,135, and 2,286 videos, filtered via Gephi to 191 then manually to 158), with manual classification of an initial sample (23 M&D videos from 158, classified Feb 11-18, 2020) and a secondary sample from identified channels (29 M&D videos, classified Mar 12-20, 2020).
integrity_note: All numerical values reconcile: 23 initial + 29 secondary = 52 total M&D videos; upload year counts (23 in 2018 + 7 in 2017 + 6 in 2019 + 2 in 2016 + 5 in 2015 + 3 in 2014/earlier + 2 in 2011 + 4 in 2010) sum exactly to 52; Table 1 lists exactly 8 verified channels as stated in the text; extraction counts (1,714 + 2,135 + 2,286 = 6,135) are consistent with the stated filtering to 191 and then 158 videos. Methods are specific with exact dates (Feb 10, 2020 collection; Feb 11-18 and Mar 12-20, 2020 classification), named tools (YouTube Data Tools, Gephi, Tor browser), and search parameters. Venue is legitimate (Frontiers in Communication, DOAJ-indexed, CORE, topic-appropriate). No signals of fabrication, predatory publishing, AI-generated text, or data manipulation detected.

design: Content analysis of 685 Google search engine results pages (SERPs) for four COVID-19-related keywords ('COVID-19', 'Coronavirus', 'SARS-CoV-2', 'fake news') across nine countries, collected between March 30 and April 27, 2020, using local Google domains with cleared cookies and no VPN to characterize website typology and information content.
integrity_note: The underlying data tables (Table 1, Table 3) are largely internally consistent—rows sum to country totals and column totals sum to the grand total of 685—suggesting the data likely exist as collected. However, there are multiple specific numerical mismatches between the prose and the tables: the abstract reports 35/635 for scientific journals (should be 34/685 per Table 1); section 3.1 reports 34/685 for non-profit websites (should be 31/685); Table 2 shows Italy news at 40% when 28/60 = 46.7%; and section 3.6 reports 1% (18/153) for testimonials in fake-news SERPs when 18/153 = 11.8%. These discrepancies require human verification to confirm the data were accurately transcribed from collection sheets rather than fabricated or misreported.

design: Qualitative content analysis of 433 posts identified as containing Ukraine-related disinformation from seven pro-government Belarusian Telegram channels monitored during 2024 (January–December for five channels, July–December for two), coded by four trained human coders with principal-investigator verification.
integrity_note: Table 3 monthly counts sum to 252, not the stated 433 total disinformation posts, and three theme rows have percentages inconsistent with their monthly counts (e.g., 'Low morale' listed as 4.6% of 433 ≈ 20 posts but monthly counts sum to 11). Additionally, footnotes 11 and 12 cite the same Telegram URL (t.me/drugoeeto/15142) for two different outlier posts described as having 1.5M and 400k views. These numerical and citation inconsistencies suggest possible data misreporting or subset confusion that requires verification against the underlying Figshare dataset before the data can be trusted as reported.

design: A descriptive quantitative online survey (Google Forms) of 140 volunteer university students at the University of Alicante, conducted between May and October 2024, measuring information sources, trust in social media, verification habits, and thematic interests regarding fake news.
integrity_note: Multiple irreconcilable data inconsistencies indicate the results cannot be trusted as reported: Table 8 manipulation question sums to 138/140 (98.6%); Table 10 reports variable n (117-140) but calculates all percentages on n=140 (e.g., 51/117=43.6% not 36.4%); the Discussion cites '38% de los encuestados' for fake news diffusion with no source in the Results; Conclusions reference topics absent from Table 10; a cyberviolence reference is cited to support fake news claims; and no ethics committee approval is documented for the human-subjects survey.

design: The study collected YouTube metadata (10,724 videos and 2,585,367 comments/replies) via the YouTube API from 1 January to 11 March 2020, manually annotated a stratified sample of 429 videos and 10,400 comments with three coders, trained BERT classifiers on the annotated data plus external fact-checked statements, and constructed directed networks to compute E-I homogeneity indices.
integrity_note: All reported counts and percentages reconcile exactly: 681,811 misinformation comments + 1,903,556 non-misinformation comments = 2,585,367 total; 376 misinformation videos + 10,348 non-misinformation videos = 10,724 total; Table 1 sums to 429 videos (34+395) and 10,400 comments (796+9,604) as stated in the text; Table 2 sums to 962 fact-checked entries; the 80/20 train-test split (632/158 videos, 1,273/319 comments) matches the balanced dataset sizes (790 and 1,592). The venue is a legitimate, Scopus-indexed Elsevier journal (Online Social Networks and Media), the methodology is detailed and reproducible (API parameters, stratified sampling, Fleiss' Kappa, BERT hyperparameters), and the prose is coherent academic writing with verifiable references. No signals of fabrication, predatory publishing, or data manipulation detected.

design: Cross-sectional content analysis of 171 TikTok videos posted between 29 June 2022 and 29 June 2023, scraped on 29 June 2023 via Apify using five diabetes-related hashtags, and rated by seven researchers using DISCERN and PEMAT-A/V instruments in REDCap.
integrity_note: Published in Clinical Diabetes (American Diabetes Association, core journal), with clear ethics exemption, specific dates (scrape on 29 June 2023), named instruments (DISCERN, PEMAT-A/V), and a coherent flowchart (399→171) that reconciles with the text. All percentages in Table 2 match their counts (e.g., 78/171=45.6%, 64/171=37.4%) and rows sum to 171. The only discrepancy is a likely typographical error in the text (n=3 vs. Table 2's n=2 for the 'no relation' group), which does not undermine the overall data integrity given the consistent totals (171 videos, 165 analyzed).

design: In June 2009, researchers searched Google, Yahoo, and Bing for U.S. hookah establishment websites, identified 367 sites with web links, and conducted a qualitative content analysis of 144 stand-alone websites from June 2009 to June 2010 using a 36-code codebook with two independent coders (Cohen’s κ = 0.93 on 20% of sites).
integrity_note: Published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine (Elsevier, core journal, 76 citations) with consistent author affiliations (University of Pittsburgh, University of Florida, American University of Beirut) and a plausible, well-documented methodology. All reported percentages based on n=144 reconcile correctly with their counts within standard rounding (e.g., 114/144=79.2%→79%, 59/144=41.0%→41%). The only discrepancy is in Figure 1, where the listed exclusion reasons sum to 220 rather than the stated 223, a minor arithmetic error that does not affect the reported final sample of 144. No signals of fabrication, predatory venue, topic mismatch, or machine-generated text were detected.

design: The study collected vaccine-related news content and engagement metrics from 682 Italian news outlets (96 newspapers, 462 online-only outlets, 89 TV channels, 35 radio channels) across Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and YouTube from January 1, 2016 to December 31, 2021 using CrowdTangle and official platform APIs, plus Twitter retweet data from January 2020 to December 2021 to analyze audience overlap.
integrity_note: All quantitative claims reconcile perfectly: Table 1 counts sum to totals (161+521=682 outlets; 44,547+308,983=353,530 contents; 10,898,774+84,332,137=95,230,911 interactions) and all percentages match their bases (e.g., 161/682=23.6%, 44,547/353,530=12.6%, 10,898,774/95,230,911=11.4%). Venue is PNAS Nexus (Oxford University Press, DOAJ-indexed, core journal, National Academy of Sciences), not predatory. Methodology is specific and plausible (CrowdTangle/Twitter/YouTube APIs, BERT fine-tuning with 80/20 split, MCMC with H=5,000 and 1,000 burn-in, 206 nodes/1,555 edges after thresholding). Text is coherent academic prose with real, relevant references; no AI-filler, no topic/venue mismatch, no impossible splits. Received Feb 13 2024, accepted Oct 8 2024 (8 months, reasonable for this venue).

design: The study collected mixed-methods data on three TikTok activist hashtag campaigns (#TolakOmnibusLaw, #MakeSchoolASaferPlace, #JunkTerrorBill) in Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines during 2020–2021, comprising qualitative content analysis of 150 videos, semi-structured interviews with 12 creators, systematic fact-checking of video claims, and manual scraping of 7,500 comments (refined to 5,155) for sentiment and hate speech analysis.
integrity_note: The paper appears genuine (legitimate SAGE journal Social Media + Society, real author Nuurrianti Jalli with verifiable publication record, real campaigns with specific dates/handles, and mostly internally consistent Table 2 percentages), but contains a significant numerical inconsistency: the aggregate sentiment counts in the text (2,881 neutral/273 positive/2,001 negative) contradict the country-by-country sums in Table 2 (2,966/240/1,949) that the text explicitly cites as the source. Additionally, the mention of 'three IFCN-certified professional fact-checkers in the research team' in a single-author paper without acknowledgment, and the complete absence of any ethics approval statement for interviews with activists in repressive environments, warrant human review to verify data provenance and reporting accuracy.

design: Survey data were collected from 171 university students in Singapore (aged 18–29) via paper questionnaires distributed on two public university campuses in 2015, measuring self-reported misinformation sharing prevalence and 29 reasons for sharing on a 7-point Likert scale.
integrity_note: All reported percentages reconcile exactly with their counts and bases: 171/200 = 85.5% response rate, 98/171 = 57.3% female, 73/171 = 42.7% male, and 116/171 = 67.8% sharing prevalence. The t-test degrees of freedom (169) correctly equal n−2 for the total sample of 171, and the reported means, SDs, and group sizes yield a t-value (~2.18) consistent with the reported p = .029. The venue is the reputable ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries (JCDL'15) with a valid ACM DOI (10.1145/2756406.2756941), 86 citations, and authors affiliated with Nanyang Technological University. The text contains specific, verifiable details (grant number RG58/14, specific misinformation example, precise rankings of 29 items) and no signs of AI-generated filler, predatory publishing, or data fabrication.

design: The authors collected English-language tweets containing the terms “yellow fever” and “treatment” or “cure” posted between December 1, 2015 and February 1, 2017, classified them as medically correct or misinformation, and analyzed the links posted in the tweets.
integrity_note: The percentages reported for misleading (61.3%) and correct (38.7%) tweets are inconsistent with the reported counts (n=233 and n=144) out of the stated total of 377 (actual values: 61.8% and 38.2%). This internal numerical mismatch requires verification, though the venue (American Journal of Infection Control, Elsevier, CORE-indexed), the authentic-looking sample tweets in Table 1, and the coherent search methodology suggest a genuine study with a likely typographical error rather than fabricated data.

design: A cross-sectional representative survey of N=1,140 German adults (743 panel participants from a 2017 wave plus 397 newly recruited stratified participants) was conducted via computer-assisted web interviews in March 2020 by Kantar-Emnid, measuring self-reported reactions to fabricated political disinformation images and psychological predictors (populist attitudes, anger, injustice perceptions, participatory efficacy, alternative media use).
integrity_note: The paper appears in a legitimate, indexed top-tier journal (Computers in Human Behavior) with verifiable authors, funding (BMBF grant 16KIS0496), and a named professional data-collection agency (Kantar-Emnid), and the method is described in sufficient detail to suggest genuine data collection. However, there are multiple internal numerical inconsistencies that a human should verify: the text reports β = .17 for populist attitudes→anger while Table A4 shows .68; the text reports alternative media→anger as β = .07, p < .05 while the table shows .05, p = .07; the Johnson-Neyman upper bounds (2.70 vs 2.29) are swapped between constructs in different paragraphs; and the education percentages sum to 99.44% and do not match integer counts of N=1,140. These are likely reporting/typographical errors rather than fabrication, but they prevent full reconciliation of the text with the tables.

design: Public Twitter/X tweets (Jan 1, 2020–Dec 31, 2022) were collected via the Twitter API using hashtags/keywords derived from British American Tobacco and Philip Morris International industry tweets, filtered from 3,436,070 to 842,754 tobacco-related tweets, topic-modeled with LDA into 6 topics, and coded for misinformation by humans and ChatGPT on samples of 600 (S1) and 8,427 (S2) tweets.
integrity_note: Core pipeline numbers are internally consistent and look genuine (3,436,070 -> 842,754; Table 1 topic sizes sum exactly to 842,754; S2 = 1% of each topic sums to 8,427; 121/557 = 21.7% is correct), and the venue (BMC Public Health, DOAJ/CORE, BioMed Central) matches the topic with no pay-to-publish or scope-mismatch signal. However, the results tally cannot be reconciled: the final misinformation set is stated as 169 although its components 58 + 121 = 179 (and the text later says 179), the source counts 79+45+12+12+31 = 179 are described as 'out of the 169', and the three falsehood types 30+122+44 = 196 exceed the stated total. These are reporting inconsistencies in the results rather than proof of fabrication, so a human should verify the 169/179/196 counts before the paper is used.

design: The study collected Reddit comments from January 2016 to December 2019 authored by ~3M U.S.-geolocated users mentioning S&P 500 companies, labeled news domains for credibility using external lists, gathered monthly adjusted stock prices (2014–2019) and Glassdoor reviews (2008–2020), and conducted an Amazon Mechanical Turk crowdsourcing study (103 participants, 1,500 articles) to categorize fake news articles during defined 'misinformation shocks'.
integrity_note: Paper is from ICWSM 2024 (AAAI) with verifiable authors and detailed, plausible methods, but contains three numerical inconsistencies between text and tables (1.4M vs 12.8K fake news comments; 16% vs 17% calculation; 126 vs 114 targeted companies) that appear to be typographical errors but require human verification.

design: The study collected approximately 1.3 million Italian-language YouTube comments from over 345,000 users on 30,436 COVID-19-related videos across 7,157 channels (videos from 01/12/2019 to 21/04/2020, comments from 15/01/2020 to 15/06/2020) using the YouTube Data API, and manually annotated 70,413 comments for hate speech using eight double-annotators.
integrity_note: The paper is published in Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio), a legitimate indexed journal (DOAJ, CORE), with verifiable author affiliations at reputable institutions (Ca' Foscari, Jožef Stefan Institute, Sapienza). The methodology is detailed and plausible (YouTube Data API, AGCOM source list, double annotation with Krippendorff's Alpha, AlBERTo transformer model), and the prose is coherent with genuine references. design: The study collected approximately 65 million original Twitter posts (36 million hurricane-related and 29 million climate-change-related) and 240,000 news articles via the official Twitter API between January and May 2022, covering the period January 1, 2010 to December 31, 2021.
integrity_note: Published in PLOS Climate (DOAJ-indexed, core journal) by authors from reputable institutions (The Alan Turing Institute, Ca' Foscari University, etc.). Methods are detailed and plausible (official Twitter API, specific collection window Jan-May 2022, BERTopic, NewsGuard). However, there is a significant numerical inconsistency: the stated 2% geolocation rate of the 29M climate tweets (~580k geolocated tweets) cannot reconcile with Table 1's out-of-location counts (hundreds of thousands per hurricane, summing to ~4.6M). Additionally, the abstract's '2010 to 2022' conflicts with the methods' '2010 to 2021' data range. These may be typographical errors, but the geolocation discrepancy requires human verification before the data can be trusted as reported.

design: Digital footprints (posts, follower counts, verification status, friend counts and friend lists) from the first one million registered Sina Weibo users were obtained from a data company, filtered by the keyword 'genetically modified' (转基因) to yield 9070 posts spanning March 2010–September 2014; 3592 of these were manually coded by four coders for attitude, rumor veracity, and topic, with 2096 posts achieving coder agreement (posted by 1153 users) used for analysis.
integrity_note: The paper appears in a legitimate Elsevier journal (Telematics and Informatics) with verifiable authors, real-world events (2012 French rat study, 2014 Wuhan Bt63 rice report, Cui Yongyuan documentary), and internally consistent core counts (338+1758=2096; 213+940=1153). However, multiple numerical mismatches exist: topic percentages sum to 95.79% instead of 100%; the text reports a negative-attitude coefficient of 2.6082 while Table 4 shows 2.7587; Table 3 lists Hubert Gamma as 131.000 (impossible for a correlation, likely a decimal-point error); and the reported network density (0.007) does not match the stated 230 nodes/258 edges (~0.0098). These are likely reporting typos rather than fabricated data, but they warrant human verification before inclusion.

design: The study collected descriptive advertising data on 5,485 websites from 2019-2021 using Oracle Moat Pro crawlers combined with misinformation ratings from NewsGuard and GDI, plus two survey experiments: a consumer experiment with 4,039 U.S. internet users recruited via CloudResearch and a decision-maker experiment with 442 executives/managers from Stanford and CMU executive education alumni, both conducted with IRB approval and pre-registration in 2023-2024.
integrity_note: This is a legitimate NBER working paper from established researchers at Stanford/CMU with detailed, internally consistent methodology. Key counts reconcile (e.g., 3,811+6,499=10,310 websites; 1,276+4,209=5,485 final sample; 806+808+802+809+814=4,039 consumer participants; 216+226=442 decision-makers). IRB protocols and pre-registration are provided. Three minor text-vs-table discrepancies exist (49% vs 56% executive role; 44.5% vs 53.0% platform beliefs; 44% of 42,595 vs Table A2 sum of 71,159) but appear to be clerical, definitional, or due to multi-industry classification rather than evidence of data fabrication. No signals of predatory venue, impossible splits, or AI-generated text.

design: Cross-sectional random-quota online survey of the German adult population (final N=967) conducted by the commercial panel Respondi between March 26 and April 8, 2020, measuring self-reported alternative counter-news use, fake news recall, and dispositional worldview variables (conspiracy mentality, media trust, political extremity, right-wing authoritarianism).
integrity_note: Published in Digital Journalism (Taylor & Francis, SSCI-indexed) with verifiable author affiliations and OSF pre-registration; all reported percentages (e.g., 470/967=49%, 116/967=12%, 146/967=15.1%, 781/967=80.8%) are internally consistent with N=967, indicating the data likely exist as reported. However, two numerical anomalies require human verification: (1) the political leaning SD is reported as 13.96 on a 1–10 scale, which is mathematically impossible and appears copied from the age variable; (2) the sample exclusion flow (1455 → 399 → 26 → 464 → 967) does not sum correctly as written, though N=967 is used consistently throughout the results.

design: Web browsing history records from 636 US social media users recruited via Facebook ads between March 28 and April 30, 2018, paired with survey self-reports, covering a 90-day browsing period.
integrity_note: The paper is published in a legitimate core journal by established scholars and provides a data availability statement (Harvard Dataverse). Recruitment and sample-flow numbers reconcile internally (e.g., 3,735/266,827=1.4%; 553/636=87%; 86,028+52,128+25,670=163,826). However, there are internal numerical inconsistencies that a human should verify: Figure 2 caption (n=136,923) contradicts the text (163,826 visits); the 3.4% (2,413) URL-tag recovery rate is mathematically inconsistent with the 90% coverage claim; 209/636=32.9% is reported as 32%; and the 77%/78% 'dissimilar' exposure figures for direct/hyperlinks contradict the 43% figure for direct access given earlier. These appear to be reporting errors rather than fabrication, given the detailed, verifiable methodology and data sharing.

design: National survey of 1,615 Brazilian internet users (18+) conducted May 21–July 3, 2019 by Ibope using online panel (N=1,431) and random digit dial (N=184) interviews with demographic quotas for region, age, gender, and education.
integrity_note: The venue is legitimate (DOAJ-indexed, established authors, real DOI) and the study design is described in credible detail, but the Methods section reports statistically impossible values for multiple 5-point Likert scales (e.g., SD=13.06, mean=5.75 on a 1–5 scale), which the Results section contradicts with plausible values (mean=3.91). Additionally, Figure 3 percentages (62% FB, 67% WA for often/always misinformation) contradict the text (66% FB, 50% WA) and reverse the reported platform difference, the Instagram chi-square statistic (4.18) is inconsistent with its reported p-value (0.01), and Table 1 column percentages sum to 166%. These internal contradictions suggest either severe data-processing errors or fabricated statistics in parts of the paper, requiring human verification against raw data before inclusion.

design: The authors collected Twitter data via the public API during the 2019 Danish national election (captures between 28 May and 6 June 2019), sampling 7,005 unique user accounts from the #dkpol and #fv19 hashtags (retrieving up to 200 recent tweets each, yielding 1.1 million tweets), plus separate datasets of 196,000 tweets from party supporters, 2,300 from official party accounts, and up to 200 tweets from each of 362 active candidates, to detect misinformation through temporal, spatial, and multi-language analysis.
integrity_note: The paper is a genuine TTO 2019 conference paper from IT University of Copenhagen with detailed, specific data (account names, location counts, language counts, exact timestamps) and legitimate references. The only numerical issue is a minor internal inconsistency: the stated 59.2% coverage does not match the stated 1,046/1,788 hours (which yields 58.5%), and the 1,788-hour figure appears inconsistent with the stated 7 May–5 June date range; these appear to be typographical errors rather than fabricated data, as all other percentages (25.8%, 0.67%, 1%, 0.001%) reconcile correctly with their counts and bases.

design: Computational content analysis of Corona-related Facebook posts collected via CrowdTangle from January 7 to March 22, 2020, comprising 2,446 posts from 32 German alternative news media pages (plus 18,051 mainstream and 282 fact-checking posts for comparison), analyzed using LDA topic modeling (k=11), named-entity co-occurrence analysis, and dictionary-based matching against fact-checker debunks.
integrity_note: All quantitative claims reconcile with their stated bases: 2,446 alternative posts / 32 pages = 76 posts per page; 589,534 interactions / 2,446 posts = 241 interactions per post; 16,779,317 mainstream likes / 1,653,208 alternative likes = 10.15× (reported as 'more than ten times'); 215,119 / 51,663 = 4.16× per page (reported as 'slightly more than four times'); t-test df = 2,446 + 18,051 − 2 = 20,495 matches the reported t(20495); 25% fewer interactions per post (241 vs. 318; (318−241)/318 = 24.2%). The venue is a legitimate arXiv preprint (cs.SI) from a recognized university working-paper series (MOR, University of Münster); author affiliations and emails are consistent; the methodology (CrowdTangle public-page crawling, LDA with k=11 validated by ldatuning, Stanford CoreNLP NER, co-occurrence filtering) is specific and reproducible; no AI-filler prose, topic/venue mismatch, or impossible data patterns detected.

design: Daily Google SERPs were collected for 420 US House member name queries from 436 simulated locations (435 congressional districts + DC) from September 1 to December 31, 2020, reduced to 112 days after excluding 10 missing days, yielding 20,087,638 searches, 302,459,959 results, and 4,229 unique domains.
integrity_note: Not SUSPECT: the venue is DOAJ/core, the methods are specific, and the core counts reconcile (420×436×112≈20.5M before failures; 20,087,638 searches; 302,459,959/20,087,638=15.06; Table A2 rows sum to 302,459,959 results and 4,229 domains; Table 1 rows sum to their totals). But there are real reporting mismatches beyond rounding: NewsGuard unmatched is stated as 22.8% while 76.6% matched/Table A3 implies 23.4%; Appendix D gives local-news CI [7.6, 13.9] whereas Table A6 gives 39.1–57.3; and 187/420 rounds to 44.5%, not 44.6%. These look like typos/forced-sum rather than fabricated data, but a human should verify the affected sentences and tables.

design: Three-wave panel surveys of representative samples of Americans conducted by the GfK Group (KnowledgePanel) during the 2012 and 2016 U.S. Presidential elections (July–November 2012 and July–November 2016), measuring self-reported social media use for political information and belief accuracy regarding candidate falsehoods (2012) and campaign issue falsehoods (2016).
integrity_note: Published in PLoS ONE (DOAJ-indexed, core journal, 186 citations) with a valid DOI and public data availability statement (Harvard Dataverse). Single-author paper by an established scholar (R. Kelly Garrett, Ohio State University) with NSF funding (IIS-1149599) and explicit IRB approval (Study 2012B0247). Data collection is described with specific dates, sample sizes (N=1,004/783/652 for 2012; N=965/763/625 for 2016), and a named commercial panel provider (GfK KnowledgePanel). Statistical reporting includes specific test statistics (e.g., Hausman χ2(6)=15.87, p=0.015) and confidence intervals. Table percentages (Tables 1 and 2) are plausible given the reported wave-3 Ns (652 and 623) and show no internal contradictions; completion rates are consistent with response rates among invited respondents rather than simple retention. Prose is academic, specific, and supported by relevant, verifiable citations. No signals of predatory venue, topic mismatch, AI-generated filler, or fabricated data.

design: The authors collected 446 million election-related tweets via Twitter's V1.1 streaming API between September and December 2022 using keyword lists, then curated a subset of 1.81 million tweets corresponding to 135 identified rumors about the 2022 U.S. midterm elections, supplemented with backfilled tweets and manual rumor identification by research assistants.
integrity_note: The paper appears to be a genuine, detailed dataset paper from a legitimate venue (Journal of Quantitative Description: Digital Media, DOAJ-indexed, core) with real authors from recognized institutions and a coherent, detailed methodology. However, there is a significant numerical inconsistency: Table 4 percentages for domain prevalence imply a base of ~315,600 tweets containing links, but the text states 273,965 tweets (15.13%) contain links. The counts in Table 4 (e.g., 45,622 for thepostmillennial.com) do not reconcile with the stated base of 273,965 (which would yield 16.65%, not 14.46%). This mismatch suggests an error in either the reported count of link-containing tweets or in the Table 4 percentages/counts. Additionally, a date typo (2023 instead of 2022) appears in the rumor criteria section. These issues warrant human review to determine if they are calculation errors or indicate deeper problems, but do not by themselves prove fabrication.

design: An online quantitative survey claiming 252 responses from Azad Jammu and Kashmir residents about Facebook disinformation and fear during the May 2025 Pakistan-India war, conducted via 'opportunity sampling' through digital networks with no dates, ethics approval, or instrument details provided.
integrity_note: Multiple irreconcilable numerical errors indicate the data likely do not exist as reported: Table 1 sums to 220 not 252 and 145/252=57.5% not 65.3%; Table 2 sums to 253; 244/252=96.8% not 97.2%; text contradicts tables on key percentages (44.4% vs 47.6% vs 45.6%). Venue shows hijacked/predatory signals: journal name 'Social Science Review Archives' but URL policyjournalofms.com, not in DOAJ/CORE, 0 citations, empty publisher field. Reference contains '7800010 Bytes'. Repetitive passages suggest AI generation. No ethics approval or data collection dates for a study of the May 2025 war published in the Oct-Dec 2025 issue, indicating an implausibly fast editorial process.

design: A mixed-methods study claiming to survey 60 social media users in Ilala Municipal, Tanzania and interview TCRA officials in 2024, using questionnaires and interviews analyzed via 'thematic analysis via SPSS'.
integrity_note: The paper exhibits multiple integrity red flags indicating the data likely cannot be trusted as reported: (1) the venue is not indexed in DOAJ or CORE and has a generic title consistent with predatory publishing; (2) the methods section claims 'thematic analysis via SPSS', which is methodologically impossible (SPSS is for quantitative statistics, not qualitative thematic analysis), suggesting the analysis was not conducted as described; (3) the literature review contains near-duplicate paragraphs with only synonym substitutions, and the text includes a disclaimer denying AI use despite obvious AI-generated characteristics (duplicated text, generic prose, grammatical errors); (4) the reference list contains multiple duplicate entries and garbled citations; (5) numerical inconsistencies exist between text and tables (0.5% vs 5.0% for 'other sources'; 16.6% vs 16.7% for rarely/never fact-checking). While the frequency tables are internally consistent, the combination of incoherent methodology, likely AI-generated text with a false disclaimer, and questionable venue makes it probable the study was not conducted or reported as claimed.

design: The study collected mixed-methods data (semi-structured questionnaires and interview schedules) from 195 respondents in Nyeri County, Kenya—185 adult residents recruited via purposive/random sampling and 10 journalists/politicians via simple random sampling—regarding fake news witnessed during the 2022 general elections; data collection dates and ethics approval are not reported.
integrity_note: The paper contains multiple fatal internal contradictions: the text states the total population is 280 while Table 1 shows 470,773; the abstract claims 195 respondents were calculated via Fisher's formula but the calculation yields 185; and 87% of respondents reporting fake news on Facebook exceeds the 70.8% who reported social media as a source (logically impossible). Additionally, the study reports a 100% response rate and 100% of respondents witnessing fake news, multiple references do not match in-text citations (e.g., 'Butler Horton, 2018' vs a 2021 agricultural dissertation; 'Garett et al., 2019' vs a 2018 sleep study), and the text contains template language ('your study can shed light'). These signals indicate the data are likely not real or not as reported.

design: A pilot survey of 132 respondents in Ahmedabad district, Gujarat, India (2022) using a questionnaire on fake news awareness, verification methods, and opinions on government regulation, analyzed via Cramer's V association coefficients.
integrity_note: Severe topic/venue mismatch: a mass-communication/misinformation study published in the 'Journal for ReAttach Therapy and Developmental Diversities' (eISSN 2589-7799, not in DOAJ, no publisher listed), matching the predatory/hijacked venue pattern. Internal statistical inconsistencies: text reports Cramer's V = 0.334 for profession/awareness but Table 1 shows 0.278; text reports 0.281 for profession/specific-agenda but the table shows 0.156. Multiple percentage miscalculations beyond rounding (e.g., 13/132 reported as 9.80% instead of 9.85%; 2/132 as 1.50% instead of 1.52%). Identical quotation attributed to both Potter (2013) and Baran (2004); references 1 and 2 are duplicate URLs. No ethics approval mentioned. These signals indicate the data and text cannot be trusted as reported.

design: The paper claims to have collected quantitative survey data from 400 Nigerian adults residing in Edo State via an online questionnaire in 2023, alongside qualitative interview data that is mentioned in the abstract and methods but never reported in the results.
integrity_note: Multiple red flags indicate the data may not exist as reported: (1) predatory venue (IJISRT, not in DOAJ) with metadata mismatch (Zenodo/CERN vs IJISRT in PDF); (2) abstract uses future tense for interviews ('will be conducted') while reporting findings, and claims mixed methods while methodology claims quantitative-only; (3) qualitative data is mentioned but never reported; (4) reference [1] cites a paper with the identical title to this article; (5) repetitive AI-like boilerplate text throughout the literature review and impact sections; (6) no ethics approval number, IRB reference, or specific data collection dates provided; (7) minor percentage mismatches in Tables 4 (6.6% vs 6.5%) and 11 (18.1% vs 18.0%).

design: The study collected web-scraped data from three sources covering 2019–2022: 8,040 tweets from Bolsonaro’s account (@desbloqueandoJB), 6,685 false speeches catalogued by the Aos Fatos agency, and 388 fake news items verified by the TSE “Fato ou Boato” consortium, which were keyword-filtered to 932 items and manually reduced to 453 contents for classification of attacks on electronic voting machines.
integrity_note: All quantitative claims reconcile with their stated bases: Table 2 rows sum correctly (8,040+6,685+388=15,113; 101+478+353=932; 21+162+270=453), Bolsonaro’s 183 attacks equal 21 tweets + 162 speeches, and every reported percentage matches its count when recomputed (80/183=43.72%, 25/183=13.66%, 105/183=57.38%, 71/270=26.30%, 60/270=22.22%, 39/270=14.44%, 37/270=13.70%, 64.07% of 270=173, 21.48% of 270=58, 9.26% of 270=25, 3.70% of 270=10, 1.48% of 270=4, and 253/453=55.85%). The venue is the legitimate ACM-published ICEGOV 2023 conference, authors are affiliated with recognized Brazilian institutions (FGV EAESP, UDESC ESAG), and the text contains specific dated source materials (e.g., “live: 29 jul. 2021”, “August 12, 2022”) and named Python scraping tools consistent with genuine data collection.

design: Observational study collecting all messages (text, images, videos, audio, URLs) from 141 and 364 publicly accessible Brazilian political WhatsApp groups during the 2018 truck drivers' strike (May 21–June 2, 2018) and presidential election campaign (Aug 16–Oct 7, 2018), respectively, by discovering invitation links via Google/Twitter/Facebook, joining groups with cell phones using a custom tool, and periodically downloading shared content.
integrity_note: Paper is from WWW 2019 (ACM), a top-tier venue, with verifiable authors (UFMG, MPI-SWS, IBM) and 327 citations. Methodology is specific and consistent with known WhatsApp monitoring studies (Garimella et al. tool, public group links, specific 2018 dates). Numerical discrepancies (URL percentages, Table 5 unique image count, user percentage denominator) appear to be minor reporting errors or extraction artifacts rather than fabrication, given the paper's provenance and that other counts reconcile (e.g., text+images+videos+audios sum to total messages; fact-checking counts 17+5=22 and 17/47=36.2% are correct). No signals of predatory venue, AI-filler, or impossible data.

design: The study scraped 19,053 first-level reader comments from 2,841 COVID-19-tagged articles on Maroela Media on 21 February 2023 using Octoparse, filtered them via keyword search and manual verification to 572 comments containing conspiracy theories or fake news, translated them to English with Google Translate, and applied computational topic modelling (word co-occurrence networks with the Louvain algorithm) to identify themes.
integrity_note: All reported counts are internally consistent: 19,053 comments / 2,841 articles = 6.71 (matches Table 1); 19,053 / 1,804 users = 10.56 (matches Table 1); 572 / 19,053 = 3.00% (matches the '3%' stated in §5.1). The venue (Tydskrif vir Geesteswetenskappe, published by the Academy of Science of South Africa) is a legitimate national humanities journal, not predatory. The methodology is transparent (Octoparse scraping on a specific date, named keyword list, manual verification, Google Translate, nocodefunctions.com implementation of the Louvain algorithm). Verbatim reader comments carry specific dates (2020–2022) and contextual details (ANC, VIGS-pandemie, Maroela Media ownership) that indicate genuine data collection. No signs of AI-generated prose, impossible splits, or venue/topic mismatch.

design: The study collected N = 8,020,314 Epstein-related posts from Twitter, Reddit, Gab, and 4chan between August 8 and August 26, 2019 (with Reddit crawled on September 1, 2019) via platform APIs and archives, and manually coded a random sample of n = 300 posts for unwarranted conspiracy theories.
integrity_note: Published in Social Science Computer Review (SAGE, CORE-indexed), a reputable venue with matching author affiliations. All quantitative claims reconcile exactly: Table 1 platform counts (7,853,469 + 106,805 + 35,924 + 24,116) sum to the stated N = 8,020,314; time-segment percentages (4.77 + 21.40 + 73.83) sum to 100.00%; manual coding percentages (34.00% overall; 56.00%, 42.67%, 22.67%, 14.67% by platform) correspond to integer counts (102/300; 42, 32, 17, 11 of 75) that sum correctly; URL statistics (4.41% n = 13,162; 3.64% n = 10,860 of N = 298,221) match their bases; Gab user-source percentages satisfy inclusion-exclusion (52.81 + 71.77 − 24.58 = 100.00). Methods specify exact dates, tools (tweepy, PRAW), archives (4plebs.org), and inter-coder reliability (α = .89). Verbatim post quotes include specific timestamps. Minor typos (e.g., 'April' for August 2019; 'Gap' for Gab) are textual errors, not fabrication signals.

design: Online survey data collected via the Respondi panel using Qualtrics in France, Germany, Spain, and the United Kingdom between March 3 and March 30, 2020, yielding a final sample of 18,581 respondents after quality screening.
integrity_note: The paper is a CESifo Working Paper (No. 9066) distributed via SSRN, authored by researchers from reputable institutions (University of Oxford, ifo Institute, TU Dresden, etc.); the venue is legitimate and not predatory. All sample-size counts in Table 1 sum exactly to N=18,581, and the country-specific counts (5,056 + 4,529 + 4,475 + 4,521) reconcile perfectly. Regression table Ns vary by outcome as explicitly explained in the text. The only discrepancies are minor reporting errors: the abstract/introduction cite 'around 16,000' respondents versus the actual 18,581, and the text misstates the actual Muslim population share for France (8%) and Germany (5.1%) as 'less than 5%'. These do not indicate fabricated data; the detailed 100-item questionnaire (Appendix A), specific survey dates, named panel provider (Respondi), and internally consistent descriptive statistics all support genuine data collection.
